chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
title: Budd Johnson's timeless playing
summary: Collins marvels that Johnson bridged eras and took charge as the old man in Quincy Jones's band.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You know, it's interesting Pat how over the years your playing, if you are in any way astute or studious, and try to keep up and to be abreast of what is happening, how effective it can be if you really try to do these things. And I have in mind -- I can't help but think about Buddy Johnson. You know, I just told you that I met him in the early thirties, and how at this time there was just a swing era and they -- Bud was such a great musician, until he progressed and right along with whatever was happening.
And I have in mind the band that I mentioned,

Quincy's band, when I was in Europe. I hadn't seen Budd for quite a while, and in this band they had the younger musicians, you know, the little beboppers and all of the saxophone players, and they would take their solos but when they wanted that real good mainstay, that real good solo, they would call on the old man, Budd. And he would take charge. When he got there the house would just come down because Budd was truly a great -- he is truly a great soloist. And it's just interesting how he has bridged the years. Time just did nothing but enhance his playing, you know. But you have to admire --
His style -- sure his style changed, you know.
Well, he's a modernist, you know, I mean it's just timeless. This -- he is timeless, actually.
You say when you met him other saxophonists. In other words he was one three great (Inaudible).
